description: We are a team of CSE students passionate about space, technology, and interactive software. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we developed SPHEREx Open Sky Observatory, a web platform for exploring and comparing sky observations over time. Our goal is to make astronomical data accessible through interactive visualization for students, researchers, and citizen scientists.
summary:
SPHEREx Time Machine is a web tool that lets anyone travel through time in NASA infrared images. Type a star name or sky coordinates and watch that patch of sky change like a short movie: from 2MASS (≈2000) and WISE (2010) to SPHEREx (2025–2026), and on into the predicted future.

It answers the challenge directly: coordinates in, a time series of SPHEREx images out, with blink, swipe and difference views to spot anything that moves or changes. All five test targets work: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Our Python pipeline downloads SPHEREx QR2/QR3 images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and NASA’s AWS open data, removes bad pixels and zodiacal light, aligns and stacks each visit, and measures the target’s position. It doesn’t just show motion, it measures it: Barnard’s Star moves 272″ in 26 years against 273″ expected.

This matters because most brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers comparing sky images. Our tool brings NASA’s newest all-sky survey to everyone, with no coding and no account.
details:
What it does. SPHEREx Time Machine shows how the sky changes over time in real NASA images. Pick one of eight ready-made targets, or search any star name or coordinates. The tool plays every SPHEREx observation of that place like a movie, adds older NASA images (2MASS ≈2000, WISE 2010) for a 26-year baseline, and draws the predicted path into the future.

How it works.

  1. A Python pipeline (Astropy, reproject, NumPy) finds every SPHEREx QR2/QR3 observation of a position at NASA/IPAC IRSA.
  2. It reads only the needed part of each image from IRSA or NASA’s AWS open-data copy.
  3. It removes flagged pixels and the zodiacal-light model, aligns all images on one north-up grid, and stacks each visit per detector.
  4. It records each frame’s date, detector and exact wavelength, since SPHEREx’s filter changes colour across the detector.
  5. It measures the target’s position in every frame and fits its motion.

The website (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, on GitHub Pages) shows the frames, with a draggable timeline, Blink, Swipe and Difference views, the six SPHEREx detectors as “infrared colours”, brightness and contrast controls, frame metadata, bad-pixel overlays, links to every original NASA file, and shareable URLs. A live builder server (Python, FastAPI) builds new places on request. It runs several builds in parallel, shows partial results while the rest downloads, and stops stuck downloads automatically.

Results. The tool measures motions that match the known values: Barnard’s Star 10.4″/yr (272″ over 26 years; 273″ expected), Epsilon Indi B 4.7″/yr, Kapteyn’s Star 8.6″/yr, Proxima Centauri 3.9″/yr. WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, measures 8.2–8.7″/yr and appears only at 3.8–4.4 µm, showing why SPHEREx’s wavelengths matter. The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS crosses 13.7′ in 8 hours.

Benefits and impact. Volunteers comparing sky images found most known brown dwarfs and comets, and Pluto was found the same way. This tool brings NASA’s newest all-sky survey to students, teachers and citizen scientists, with no coding, installation or account. It makes changes easy to see, and it measures them.

What makes it creative.

  • “Deep time”: SPHEREx is combined with 2MASS and WISE, so motion is obvious over 26 years.
  • A “where will it be in 2050?” slider.
  • Honest science: predictions are labelled as predictions, the wavelength is shown for every frame, and a measurement bias we found during testing was fixed.
  • Built for slow connections: parallel downloads, timeouts, and step-by-step progress.

Factors we considered.

  • We used NASA data only for all images.
  • The site works without a server for the ready-made targets.
  • It’s accessible: keyboard shortcuts, phone layout, light and dark themes.

Tools: Python, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Pillow, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Aladin Lite, GitHub Pages, Hugging Face Spaces (optional builder), and Claude Code (AI coding assistant, acknowledged in our repository).
